lessonTitle: Protein Structure and Folding: From Sequence to Haemoglobin and Misfolding Disease

blocks.text: In sickle cell disease, one codon change replaces a single glutamate with valine at position 6 of the 146-residue beta-globin chain, yet red cells deform into rigid crescents that block small vessels and cause painful crises. A protein's function is written in its sequence and exposed through its fold. This unit builds protein structure level by level and then uses haemoglobin and prion or amyloid diseases to show why folding matters.

blocks.markdown: **The idea.** A protein is a chain of amino acids that folds spontaneously (often with help) into a specific three-dimensional shape; the shape is what binds substrates, transports oxygen or provides structure. We describe four levels of structure, each built on the one before.

blocks.title: Levels of protein structure
blocks.text: Primary: the linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide (covalent) bonds. Secondary: local, regular backbone folding (alpha helix, beta sheet) stabilised by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups. Tertiary: the overall three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide, stabilised by interactions among side chains. Quaternary: the arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits in one protein.

rows: Glu-6 to Val in beta-globin of haemoglobin S
Alpha helices in myoglobin; beta sheets in silk and amyloid
Hydrophobic core, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, disulphide bonds (covalent)
Haemoglobin (two alpha and two beta chains)
blocks.caption: The four levels of protein structure.

blocks.markdown: **Secondary structure.** In an **alpha helix** the backbone coils like a spring with **3.6 residues per turn**; each carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bonds to the N-H four residues along the chain, and side chains point outwards. **Proline** has a rigid ring and no backbone N-H to donate, so it breaks the helix and introduces bends. In **beta sheets** extended strands lie side by side, hydrogen-bonded between strands, running in parallel or antiparallel directions. **Tertiary structure** is dominated by the **hydrophobic effect**: nonpolar side chains bury themselves in the core away from water, while polar and charged groups lie on the surface. Disulphide bonds between cysteine residues add covalent cross-links, mostly in secreted proteins. Heat, extreme pH or urea disrupt the non-covalent forces and **denature** the protein, destroying function without breaking peptide bonds.

blocks.title: Size of an alpha helix
blocks.prompt: An alpha helix has 3.6 residues per turn and a rise of 0.15 nm per residue. Estimate the number of turns and length of a 27-residue helix.

steps.text: Turns = residues / residues per turn = 27 / 3.6 = 7.5 turns.
Length = residues x rise per residue = 27 x 0.15 nm = 4.05 nm.

blocks.markdown: **Haemoglobin and cooperativity.** Myoglobin (a monomer in muscle) binds one O2 on a haem iron and gives a **hyperbolic** saturation curve with high affinity, suited to storing oxygen. Haemoglobin is a **tetramer (alpha2 beta2)**, each subunit carrying a haem. It exists in two quaternary states: the **T (tense)** state, with low oxygen affinity, stabilised by salt bridges and favoured when deoxygenated; and the **R (relaxed)** state, with high affinity. Binding of O2 to one haem pulls the iron into the porphyrin plane and shifts the subunits toward the R state, increasing the affinity of the remaining haems. This **cooperativity** produces a **sigmoidal** oxygen-dissociation curve: haemoglobin loads fully in the lungs and releases much of its oxygen over the small drop in partial pressure found in tissues.

rows: Increased H+ (lower pH) and increased CO2 (Bohr effect)
More oxygen unloaded in active, acid tissues
Binds in the central cavity of T state
Adaptation to altitude and chronic hypoxia
More unloading in warm exercising muscle
Binds haem with very high affinity and locks R state
Impaired unloading as well as reduced capacity
blocks.caption: Allosteric effectors of haemoglobin. A right shift means lower affinity and increased unloading.

blocks.title: Oxygen carrying capacity
blocks.prompt: A patient has haemoglobin 140 g per litre and arterial oxygen saturation 98%. Each gram of fully saturated haemoglobin carries 1.34 mL O2. Calculate the oxygen bound to haemoglobin per litre of blood, ignoring dissolved oxygen.

steps.text: Maximum capacity = 140 g/L x 1.34 mL/g = 187.6 mL per litre.
Multiply by saturation: 187.6 x 0.98 = 183.8 mL per litre.

blocks.answer: About 184 mL of O2 per litre of blood. Because the curve is sigmoidal, saturation falls only modestly until partial pressure drops substantially, protecting loading in the lungs.

blocks.markdown: **Folding and misfolding.** Most proteins fold correctly with the help of **chaperones** (such as heat-shock proteins), and misfolded proteins are tagged with ubiquitin and degraded in the proteasome. When this quality control fails, misfolded proteins can form insoluble aggregates. Two mechanisms matter. **Amyloid** diseases involve proteins that change into **beta-sheet-rich fibrils** that deposit in tissues (amyloid beta in Alzheimer disease, light chains in AL amyloidosis, transthyretin in familial amyloid); amyloid stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light. **Prion** diseases (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, kuru) are caused by the infectious misfolded form **PrPSc** of the normal cell-surface prion protein PrPC: PrPC is rich in alpha helix, PrPSc is rich in beta sheet and resistant to protease, and it **templates** conversion of more PrPC, so the disease spreads without nucleic acid. Folding defects can also cause loss of function; in cystic fibrosis the common F508 deletion causes the CFTR protein to misfold and be degraded.

blocks.title: Sequence determines structure
blocks.text: A single change in primary structure can alter folding, assembly or solubility. Haemoglobin S (Glu6Val) polymerises when deoxygenated because the new hydrophobic valine sticks to a pocket on another molecule. Prions show the reverse idea: identical sequence, different fold, completely different behaviour.

blocks.title: Link level to bond
blocks.text: Hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms mean secondary structure. Side-chain interactions mean tertiary structure. Subunit assembly means quaternary structure. Peptide bonds survive denaturation.

points: Primary structure is the sequence; secondary is backbone hydrogen-bonded helices and sheets; tertiary is the fold of one chain; quaternary is subunit assembly.
Haemoglobin shows cooperative oxygen binding through T to R transitions, giving a sigmoidal curve modulated by H+, CO2, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and temperature.
Misfolded proteins cause disease through amyloid fibril deposition or prion-type templated conversion to a beta-sheet-rich form.

questions.stem: Which interaction chiefly stabilises an alpha helix?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens
Disulphide bonds between cysteine side chains
Peptide bonds between adjacent residues
Ionic bonds between subunits

questions.correctOptionText: Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens

distractorRationale.a: Correct: backbone hydrogen bonds between residues four apart hold the helix.
distractorRationale.b: Disulphide bonds contribute to tertiary structure, not the helix itself.
distractorRationale.c: Peptide bonds make up the primary structure and are not what stabilises the helical coil.
distractorRationale.d: Ionic interactions between subunits belong to quaternary structure.

questions.explanation: In an alpha helix each carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bonds with the amide N-H four residues ahead, and the pattern is repeated along the helix. These regular backbone hydrogen bonds define secondary structure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of quaternary structure?

options.text: The four-subunit arrangement of haemoglobin
The folded globular chain of myoglobin
The sequence of amino acids in insulin
A beta sheet in a silk protein

distractorRationale.a: Correct: quaternary structure is the assembly of several polypeptide subunits, as in haemoglobin (alpha2 beta2).
distractorRationale.b: Myoglobin is one polypeptide, so its fold is tertiary structure.
distractorRationale.d: A beta sheet is secondary structure.

questions.explanation: Quaternary structure describes how separate polypeptide chains associate in one functional protein. Myoglobin is a single chain and therefore has no quaternary structure, while haemoglobin is a tetramer.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces a leucine buried in the hydrophobic core of a globular enzyme with an aspartate. What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: A charged side chain in the core destabilises the tertiary fold, risking misfolding and loss of function
The peptide backbone is cleaved at that position
The secondary structure is unaffected and the enzyme is unchanged
A new disulphide bond is formed

questions.correctOptionText: A charged side chain in the core destabilises the tertiary fold, risking misfolding and loss of function

distractorRationale.a: Correct: placing a charged group in a hydrophobic core is energetically unfavourable and disrupts folding.
distractorRationale.b: Changing a side chain does not cleave the peptide bond.
distractorRationale.c: A core substitution of this kind is likely to change the fold, not leave function untouched.
distractorRationale.d: Aspartate has no sulphur and cannot form a disulphide bond; only cysteine does.

questions.explanation: The hydrophobic effect drives nonpolar residues into the interior. Introducing a charged aspartate there disturbs the packing and is likely to destabilise tertiary structure, causing misfolding or degradation.

questions.stem: During intense exercise, muscle produces CO2 and lactic acid and its temperature rises. How do these changes affect haemoglobin in muscle capillaries?

options.text: They stabilise the T state, shift the curve to the right, and increase oxygen release
They stabilise the R state, shift the curve to the left, and decrease oxygen release
They have no effect on oxygen affinity
They convert haemoglobin to myoglobin

questions.correctOptionText: They stabilise the T state, shift the curve to the right, and increase oxygen release

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lower pH, higher CO2 and higher temperature favour the low-affinity T state, increasing unloading.
distractorRationale.b: This is the opposite of the Bohr effect and would reduce oxygen delivery to working muscle.
distractorRationale.c: These factors are allosteric effectors and clearly alter affinity.
distractorRationale.d: Haemoglobin cannot be converted into myoglobin; they are different proteins.

questions.explanation: Protons, CO2 and heat stabilise the T (tense) state of haemoglobin, lowering oxygen affinity so that oxygen is released where the tissue needs it most. This right shift of the curve is called the Bohr effect for pH and CO2.

questions.stem: Why is the oxygen-binding curve of haemoglobin sigmoidal while that of myoglobin is hyperbolic?

options.text: Oxygen binding to one haemoglobin subunit shifts the tetramer toward the R state, raising the affinity of the other subunits; myoglobin has a single site
Haemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen at every partial pressure than myoglobin because it has fewer haem groups
Myoglobin is a tetramer whose subunits compete for oxygen
Haemoglobin binds oxygen irreversibly

questions.correctOptionText: Oxygen binding to one haemoglobin subunit shifts the tetramer toward the R state, raising the affinity of the other subunits; myoglobin has a single site

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cooperativity between subunits of the tetramer produces the sigmoidal shape; the monomer binds without cooperativity.
distractorRationale.b: Haemoglobin has four haem groups, and the shape arises from cooperativity, not the number of haems.
distractorRationale.c: Myoglobin is a monomer, not a tetramer.
distractorRationale.d: Oxygen binding to haemoglobin is reversible, which is essential for delivery to tissues.

questions.explanation: In a tetramer, the conformational change induced by oxygen binding at one subunit is transmitted to the others, increasing their affinity. A monomer such as myoglobin has no such communication, so its curve is a simple rectangular hyperbola.

questions.stem: True or false: prion diseases are transmitted by a misfolded protein that converts normal protein to the abnormal form, without a nucleic acid genome.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The abnormal PrPSc, rich in beta sheet, acts as a template that induces normal PrPC to refold into the abnormal conformation. No nucleic acid is required, which is why prions resist ordinary sterilisation methods that target DNA or RNA.

questions.stem: A patient has haemoglobin 120 g per litre and arterial oxygen saturation of 95%. Each gram of fully saturated haemoglobin carries 1.34 mL of oxygen. Calculate the oxygen bound to haemoglobin in one litre of arterial blood, ignoring dissolved oxygen.
questions.unit: mL O2 per litre of blood
questions.explanation: Maximum capacity = 120 x 1.34 = 160.8 mL per litre, and 95% saturation gives 160.8 x 0.95 = 152.8 mL per litre. Anaemia reduces oxygen content because there is less haemoglobin to carry oxygen, even when saturation is normal.

questions.stem: A resting adult has haemoglobin 150 g per litre. Arterial blood is 98% saturated and mixed venous blood is 74% saturated. Using 1.34 mL of oxygen per gram of fully saturated haemoglobin, calculate the oxygen unloaded per litre of blood as it passes through the tissues.
questions.unit: mL O2 per litre of blood
questions.explanation: The fall in saturation is 0.98 - 0.74 = 0.24. Capacity is 150 x 1.34 = 201 mL per litre, so unloading = 201 x 0.24 = 48.2 mL per litre. The steep middle of the sigmoidal curve means that a modest drop in oxygen partial pressure releases this large fraction.

questions.stem: Distinguish primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary protein structure, naming the main bonds or forces that stabilise each level and giving one example.
markingGuide: Primary: amino acid sequence, peptide bonds (covalent)
Secondary: alpha helix and beta sheet stabilised by backbone hydrogen bonds
Tertiary: three-dimensional fold of one chain stabilised by hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and disulphide bonds
Quaternary: assembly of more than one polypeptide subunit, held by non-covalent forces
An appropriate example for each level, such as haemoglobin for quaternary and myoglobin for tertiary
Denaturation disrupts non-covalent forces but not peptide bonds
questions.explanation: The levels build from the sequence up to the assembled protein, with each level defined by the interactions that stabilise it. Naming the force along with the level is the key to a complete answer.

questions.stem: Describe how protein misfolding leads to disease, contrasting the mechanism of prion disease with that of amyloid deposition, and name one example of each.
markingGuide: Misfolded proteins escape chaperone and proteasome quality control and aggregate
Prion: normal alpha-helical PrPC converts to beta-sheet-rich, protease-resistant PrPSc
PrPSc acts as a template that converts further PrPC; transmissible without nucleic acid; example Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease or kuru
Amyloid: soluble protein forms insoluble beta-sheet fibrils that deposit in tissue and damage organs; example Alzheimer disease (amyloid beta) or AL amyloidosis
Amyloid stains with Congo red with apple-green birefringence
Loss-of-function misfolding such as the CFTR F508 deletion in cystic fibrosis may be mentioned
questions.explanation: Both groups of disease share conversion to a beta-sheet-rich, aggregation-prone form, but prion disease is distinguished by infectivity through templated conversion. Amyloid diseases are defined by the deposition of insoluble fibrils within tissues.
